## Why a proper fix

The same `glBegin` macro is copied into every wrapper, and every unported GL hack that uses `GL_POLYGON` will hit it: circuit, dolphin, maze3d, polytopes, polyhedra-gl, shark, sonar, sproingies, topblock, whale. A hack that nobody wraps just draws black, and the host tests only notice if the hack has a "draws something" check.

## Options

1. Patch TinyGL (`tools/tinygl_patch.py`) to handle `GL_POLYGON` itself, as a fan from the first vertex. Exact for convex polygons, which is every use I have seen in the vendored hacks. Needs the same guard as the line loop patch, so an unhandled primitive cannot overrun the vertex slots.
2. Map it in `glshim.h` (`glBegin` to a shim function), so each hack gets it with no wrapper. Simplest, but changes what every GL hack sees, so it needs Rod's say.
3. Leave it per wrapper (today's state).

## Things to settle

* Non-convex polygons: a fan is wrong for them. Check each user in the list above for concave shapes before relying on it.
* Display lists: Menger records its quads in a list, so the mapping has to apply at record time as well as at draw time.
* Rubik's decals need a polygon offset on top of the fan, which should stay in its wrapper.
* Tests: a frame test per hack that draws only polygons (Superquadrics and Menger have one now), and a `test_glshim` case for a quad and a pentagon, mutation-checked.
* Once it is fixed, delete the three local mappings and the comment in `gl.md` that explains them.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-18/gl-polygon-handle-it-once-in-the-gl-layer-instead-of-per-hack","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-18-gl_polygon-handle-it-once-in-the-gl-layer-instead-of-per","createdAt":"2026-10-19T06:11:07.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:34.194Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":"2026-10-19T22:09:15.103Z","canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"In Progress","statusType":"started","labels":["Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver","Enhancement"],"attachments":[{"id":"70c88758-d742-4393-99a2-cc2718f59465","title":"#138 GL_POLYGON: handle it once in the GL layer instead of per hack","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/138"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

`AGENTS.md` says to run the suite both ways when float code is involved (a pinned hash can fail under `-ffp-contract=off`). Running it that way on the GL batch branch (PR #139) stopped at XSpirograph, which that branch does not touch.

## What happened

From `firmware/`:

```text
REDACTED NO_COLOR=1 pio test -e native -f test_hacks
```

Result: 140 cases, 1 failed.

```text
test_hacks.c:613: test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main:
  Expected 15412848725209834749 Was 16303972679858120643. XSpirograph [FAILED]
```

The same suite without the flag passes (860 of 860 across the native suite). That test stops at the first moved hash in registry order, so every hack after XSpirograph is hidden behind it, including any pins that would also move.

## Not known

* Whether `main` fails the same way. I did not run it there, so this may be old, not something the branch caused.
* Which other hacks' pins move under the flag. See the gotcha in `AGENTS.md` about listing them all (temporarily append `name idx got=0x...` to a buffer and `TEST_FAIL_MESSAGE` it, then `git checkout` the file).

## To do

1. Run the same command on `main` and note whether XSpirograph fails.
2. List every pin that moves with `-ffp-contract=off` (the buffer trick above).
3. For each, decide: a hash that depends on FMA contraction should be a comparison against a reference copy (as the `canvas_line` and clip tests do), not a pinned hash; or the pin is a real difference in the frame.
4. {"id":"ARS-17","uuid":"70cf01b3-c260-4065-9cab-eade3d603975","title":"dump stats host times depend on unseeded random state (Drift reads 0.000 ms)","description":"## Problem

`firmware/.pio/build/dump/program stats <index>` reads `host_ms=0.0000` for
Drift on `main`, and it did the same on every run. Drift draws normally (a
300-frame dump shows its lines and points). The backtest feeds these host
times into the Speed bands, so the regenerated `docs/speed-backtest.md`
(PR #126) shows Drift at 0.000 ms (device/host ratio `inf`), Pedal falling
from 1.135 to 0.108 and Hopalong moving from the low band to medium.

An agent's review of #126 flagged it. It is not caused by #126.

## What I found

* `2d13505` (when the doc was last made): Drift 0.1023 ms.
* `origin/main`: Drift 0.0000 ms, repeatably.
* `git bisect` on the Drift reading: the first bad commit is `c4c5b61`
  ("Shim: random smooth palettes, bitmap fills, a picture for screen
  grabs", 2026-10-12). It changes what `make_smooth_colormap` draws from
  `random()`.

## Guess, not tested

`stats_main` in `firmware/native/dump_main.c` does not call `srandom`, so each
hack is timed from whatever random state the earlier code left. A hack whose
cost depends on its random start (Drift's fractal, Pedal, Hopalong) can land
in a sparse state and time as near zero. If that is right, the host time is a
single random draw, and the bands and Spearman figure depend on it.

## Possible fixes

* Seed with `srandom(1)` in `stats_main`, as the tests do. Reproducible, but
  one seed is still one draw.
* Better: time several seeds per hack and take the median, as
  `speed_backtest.measure_host` already does for runs.

Either changes what every hack's host time means, so it needs Rod's say-so.

## Check

After a fix, `Drift host_ms` is repeatable and non-zero, and
`uv run tools/speed_backtest.py` gives host times within a few per cent
between two runs.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-17/dump-stats-host-times-depend-on-unseeded-random-state-drift-reads-0000","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-17-dump-stats-host-times-depend-on-unseeded-random-state-drift","createdAt":"2026-10-16T19:14:14.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:37.222Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver","Bug"],"attachments":[{"id":"9aa46f7e-74b4-46f1-8ad7-8750d121eafb","title":"#127 dump stats host times depend on unseeded random state (Drift reads 0.000 ms)","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/127"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

{"id":"ARS-16","uuid":"685345d4-1875-491a-b91c-746e2372e50f","title":"Push overlap: review follow-ups from PR #112","description":"The whole-branch review of PR #112 (push overlap) found no Critical or
Important issues and these Minor ones, deferred.

- [ ] **Button task starvation.** The push worker runs at priority 3 on core
  0, above the 5 ms button task (priority 2). During the push's CPU copy
  (about 20 ms a frame) the sampler cannot run. `button_latch` debounces on
  wall-clock time, so a held press is not lost, but detection can slip by a
  push. Try priority 1 for the worker and compare `press_waited` in the log
  before and after (`main.cpp`, `spawnTask`).
- [ ] **Test that** `push_overlap_reset` **waits.** Deleting its `wait` call
  survives the suite, because the next `present()` waits anyway. The data
  cache reconfiguration in `hackStarted` depends on it. Test: a fake push
  blocks on a semaphore the test holds; call `reset` from a second thread and
  assert it has not returned until the push is released. Mutation-check it.
- [X] **One dropped frame per tap into an overlay.** Fixed in 65eb627 (#112). `loop()` calls
  `M5.update()` and `pollTouch()` before the step, so a tap is first seen
  there; the step then draws frame N+1 on the spare, `present()` is
  ineligible and swaps back to frame N, discarding N+1. Fix: in the
  ineligible branch swap back only when the canvas is clean; if the hack has
  drawn on it, keep `canvas->px` and let the synchronous push show it. Needs
  a test (eligible present, mark dirty, ineligible present, assert `cv.px` is
  the drawn buffer).
- [ ] **Delay credit double-counts** when a push outlasts the step: `t2 - t1`
  already includes the wait for push N-1, and `credit_us` adds its whole
  duration. Only hacks with a delay longer than their push are affected
  (Marbling, 6.6 fps); it shortens their pause. Subtract the time spent
  blocked, or note it in the header.
- [ ] **Reset before the switch.** `hackStarted` calls `push_overlap_reset`
  after `runner_next`. Safe today (the spare is never the buffer in flight)
  but nothing asserts it, and the new hack's `init` runs beside the push on
  the shared PSRAM cache. Move the reset ahead of `runner_next`.
- [ ] `push_overlap_destroy` **on FreeRTOS** could free the semaphore while
  the worker is still in its final `sem_give`. Never called on the device;
  note it in the header or join the worker first.
- [ ] **Docs.** `device-display.md` says "thirteen hacks are flagged"; drop
  the number, the `grep` it names is enough.

Related: #54, #112.

Agent note: this issue was written by Claude (an AI agent) at Rod's request.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-16/push-overlap-review-follow-ups-from-pr-112","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-16-push-overlap-review-follow-ups-from-pr-112","createdAt":"2026-10-14T19:52:30.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:38.526Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver","Chore"],"attachments":[{"id":"562edac7-d80e-45c7-be54-3dca31c4c8fe","title":"#115 Push overlap: review follow-ups from PR #112","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/115"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

{"id":"ARS-15","uuid":"8a79eeda-b710-4bd8-954b-632feaeb7ab9","title":"serial_capture.py: hold DTR/RTS low before opening the port","description":"Filed by Claude (an agent working for Rod) at his request.

`tools/serial_capture.py` opens the port with
`serial.Serial(port, 115200, timeout=1)` inside a reopen loop, so DTR and RTS
are not held low before `open()`. AGENTS.md warns that a reopen loop without
that once parked the chip in its bootloader (`boot:0x3 ... waiting for download`, screen frozen).

During the batch 4 port (#95) the agent used a scratch copy that builds an
unopened `serial.Serial()`, sets `dtr = False` and `rts = False`, then calls
`open()`. It captured cleanly across many flashes and a five-lap soak.

Fix: do the same in `serial_capture.py`, with a test that the port object has
both lines low before it is opened (a fake `serial.Serial`).","priority":{"value":3,"name":"Medium"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-15/serial-capturepy-hold-dtrrts-low-before-opening-the-port","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-15-serial_capturepy-hold-dtrrts-low-before-opening-the-port","createdAt":"2026-10-12T15:17:16.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:40.001Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver","Bug"],"attachments":[{"id":"de84a3c9-6f32-4cda-9414-81cd63294ba0","title":"#96 serial_capture.py: hold DTR/RTS low before opening the port","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/96"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

{"id":"ARS-15","uuid":"8a79eeda-b710-4bd8-954b-632feaeb7ab9","title":"serial_capture.py: hold DTR/RTS low before opening the port","description":"Filed by Claude (an agent working for Rod) at his request.

`tools/serial_capture.py` opens the port with
`serial.Serial(port, 115200, timeout=1)` inside a reopen loop, so DTR and RTS
are not held low before `open()`. AGENTS.md warns that a reopen loop without
that once parked the chip in its bootloader (`boot:0x3 ... waiting for download`, screen frozen).

During the batch 4 port (#95) the agent used a scratch copy that builds an
unopened `serial.Serial()`, sets `dtr = False` and `rts = False`, then calls
`open()`. It captured cleanly across many flashes and a five-lap soak.

Fix: do the same in `serial_capture.py`, with a test that the port object has
both lines low before it is opened (a fake `serial.Serial`).","priority":{"value":3,"name":"Medium"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-15/serial-capturepy-hold-dtrrts-low-before-opening-the-port","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-15-serial_capturepy-hold-dtrrts-low-before-opening-the-port","createdAt":"2026-10-12T15:17:16.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:40.001Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver","Bug"],"attachments":[{"id":"de84a3c9-6f32-4cda-9414-81cd63294ba0","title":"#96 serial_capture.py: hold DTR/RTS low before opening the port","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/96"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

{"id":"ARS-14","uuid":"c9285f7b-6e51-4aa3-9a2c-54fd0b35f3e4","title":"push_plan's flush cost is far too low: extra flushes cost ~0.85 ms, not 17 us","description":"*Filed by Claude, an agent working for Rod.*

`push_plan`'s cost model charges 17 µs (`PUSH_FLUSH_NS`) for each batch it flushes. On the board, each extra flush in one push cost about **0.85 ms**. The model was fitted to pushes with a single flush, so it cannot see this, and it may be splitting pushes too eagerly for every hack.

## Evidence (from #77, PR #85)

CloudLife, one pushed frame of about 464 rows, `-DTE_DIAG`:

| Push shape | push |
| -- | -- |
| One `pushImage` of the whole canvas | 27.8 ms |
| Whole rows, one row call each, one flush | 28.0 ms |
| Rows clipped to the disc, greedy grouping (3 flushes) | 24.7 ms |
| The same clipped rows in about 19 bands (the model's cheapest split) | 39.9 ms |

* Per-row calls cost nothing extra; the extra flushes are what cost. That's (39.9 - 24.7) / 16 extra flushes, about 0.95 ms each, or about 0.85 ms counting from the single-flush case.
* With the banded plan, Pyro (sparse) also got slower: push 1.56 to 2.8 ms.
* `TE_DIAG` reported the final flush call taking only 0.1 to 0.7 ms. The last flush of a push seems to finish in the background while the hack draws its next frame; earlier flushes in the same push are waited for in full.

## Why it might matter

The greedy grouping in `push_plan` splits whenever the model rates two batches cheaper than one. Charging 17 µs for a flush that really costs about 0.85 ms makes splits look far cheaper than they are. Hacks with scattered dirty rows (Pyro, Fireworkx, Lightning) may be paying for flushes the model thinks are free.

## Ideas

* Re-fit the flush cost from probes that include several flushes per push, scattered rows among them. The calibration note in `device-display.md` already says compact rectangles cannot tell the models apart.
* Model the last flush of a push as overlapping the next step, and earlier ones as serial.
* Compare the result against Pyro's current `push=` (1.43 ms on `main` since #85) before keeping any change.

## Care needed

* It changes how every hack's push is grouped, so it needs Rod's approval and an A/B on a sparse hack and a full-screen one.
* Unknown Pleasures' TE-synced push uses the same grouping (whole rows); a change in its flush count moves its timing (#68).","priority":{"value":3,"name":"Medium"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-14/push-plans-flush-cost-is-far-too-low-extra-flushes-cost-085-ms-not-17","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-14-push_plans-flush-cost-is-far-too-low-extra-flushes-cost-085","createdAt":"2026-10-11T22:35:04.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:41.776Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver","Performance"],"attachments":[{"id":"ffc44fa7-77eb-492f-b61f-ad8f51be6b8f","title":"#87 push_plan's flush cost is far too low: extra flushes cost ~0.85 ms, not 17 us","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/87"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

{"id":"ARS-10","uuid":"431cb65d-620f-4251-b4a0-abd4d9b694a2","title":"Flurry: not ported; needs GL TinyGL lacks and estimates under 1 fps","description":"Filed by Claude (an agent working under Rod's direction) during the
Flurry/Halo/Hexadrop/StonerView/XMatrix batch.

## What

Flurry was not ported. It is the one hack of the batch with no branch work.

## Why it was skipped

* It draws `NUMSMOKEPARTICLES` (3,600) blended, textured quads a frame
  (`glDrawArrays(GL_QUADS, ...)` in `flurry-smoke.c`).
* It needs GL that TinyGL here lacks: `glAlphaFunc`, `glRectd`,
  `gluBuild2DMipmaps` (a 256 by 256 luminance-alpha texture), and the
  luminance-alpha texture format itself.
* `tools/gl_budget.py` cannot read it (it handles single-file hacks), so
  this is arithmetic, not a measurement: with the tool's model of 4 us a
  vertex and 570 ns a pixel, 14,400 vertices are about 58 ms before any
  fill, and blended quads that overlap heavily cost seconds. Well under
  1 fps.

## To decide

* Is it worth trying at all? A cheaper route might be a count of particles
  far below 3,600 through a build-time patch, which changes the look.
* If yes, first teach `gl_budget.py` multi-file hacks so the estimate is a
  number, and measure one frame's fill on the host.

Source: `vendor/xscreensaver-6.16/hacks/glx/flurry*.c`.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-10/flurry-not-ported-needs-gl-tinygl-lacks-and-estimates-under-1-fps","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-10-flurry-not-ported-needs-gl-tinygl-lacks-and-estimates-under","createdAt":"2026-10-11T03:11:27.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:43.093Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver","Feature"],"attachments":[{"id":"a960a8a5-589b-46c0-967e-9dbd08ec38df","title":"#70 Flurry: not ported; needs GL TinyGL lacks and estimates under 1 fps","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/70"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

{"id":"ARS-5","uuid":"cf388783-c09e-44c4-b0a9-fa49e1f0b024","title":"Harden XFillArc and canvas_fill_polygon against signed overflow at extreme coordinates","description":"Drafted by Claude Code, working under Rod's direction.

## Summary

Extreme arguments to `XFillArc` (and `canvas_fill_polygon` generally) hit signed integer overflow, which is undefined behaviour in C. Raised by the review finding on trail 18 (PR #30). It does not block that PR or the Pacman port: no registered hack supplies such arguments, and AddressSanitizer does not catch this kind of overflow, so the current tests cannot see it.

## Reproduction

On a 64 by 64 canvas:

```c
XFillArc(dpy, 1, gc, INT_MIN, INT_MIN + 256, UINT_MAX, UINT_MAX, 0, 270 * 64);
```

Built with `-fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=undefined`:

```text
canvas.c:214:47: runtime error: signed integer overflow: -2147483648 - 2147460864 cannot be represented in type 'int'
```

## Where

* `firmware/src/core/canvas.c:214` (`canvas_fill_polygon`, which predates #30): the edge interpolation subtracts two `int` coordinates before multiplying by a `double`. Promote the operands to `int64_t` first, as the clip rules in `AGENTS.md` require.
* `firmware/src/x11shim/arc.c`: `lrintf` of a float beyond the `int` range is unspecified, so arc points for huge boxes can be garbage. Clamp before narrowing.
* Related, found in the same review and not yet ledgered as issues: `stroke_polyline` does not clip extreme coordinates (floats lose precision past about 2^20), and long axis-aligned polyline segments can come out one row thin.

## Suggested fix

1. Promote the coordinate operands in `canvas_fill_polygon` to `int64_t`.
2. Range-check generated arc coordinates before narrowing.
3. Add the reproduction above as a regression test built with UBSan, since the existing huge-arc test uses smaller sizes and only ASan.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-5/harden-xfillarc-and-canvas-fill-polygon-against-signed-overflow-at","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-5-harden-xfillarc-and-canvas_fill_polygon-against-signed","createdAt":"2026-10-09T05:51:06.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:44.519Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Bug","Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver"],"attachments":[{"id":"771e3791-2fe8-4d6f-80b5-b664a114751d","title":"#31 Harden XFillArc and canvas_fill_polygon against signed overflow at extreme coordinates","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/31"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

{"id":"ARS-7","uuid":"124ac0fc-1ba4-4656-b89d-23a03a04124b","title":"Deluxe: ideas for more than 11-13 fps","description":"Deluxe runs at 10.4-12.8 fps on the board (step 44.6-62.6 ms, push 32.5 ms).
These are ideas to get more out of it, none tried yet. Numbers are from the
Deluxe section of `tools/assessment_measured.md`.

## Where the time goes

* On the device a frame is the step and the push one after the other:
  about 47 ms plus 32.5 ms is about 80 ms, which is the 12 fps we see.
* A host profile put 94% of the original frame in the wide circles, which
  `stroke_circle` fixed (2-5 fps became 13-15 fps, opaque).
* Translucency added 13 ms a step on the board, and the mask that stops
  overlaps blending twice added another 3-5 ms, though it costs nothing on the
  host. So the host cannot rank these ideas: split the device step with a
  temporary flag that returns early from each part before changing anything.

## Ideas, biggest first

1. **Overlap the push with the next step.** Draw into a second canvas while the
   first is pushed. The step would no longer wait for the push, so the frame
   would take the longer of the two (about 47 ms, 21 fps) instead of the sum.
   This is the same push-overlap item still open for the GL hacks, and it
   would help every hack whose step is more than a few milliseconds.
2. **Shrink the mask.** Each multi-piece shape does a 27 KB `calloc` and scans
   every row and word of the canvas. Track the rows and words a shape touched,
   scan and clear only those, or keep one buffer instead of allocating each
   time (a static buffer would need the leak tests to expect it).
3. **Blend faster.** `blend_box` swaps every pixel to blend and swaps it back.
   Blending two pixels per 32-bit word, or in the swapped domain, would cut
   the per-pixel work. Long runs go through one call per run.
4. **Draw a star as one polygon.** A star is ten segments plus ten joins
   today. Filling its outline once would mean far fewer fills and no mask.
5. **Single precision in** `draw_star`**.** It does ten `cos` and ten `sin` in
   software `double` per star per frame. Small beside the rest, but a
   single-precision wrapper is cheap (`techniques.md`).
6. **Cheaper erase.** The hack fills the whole canvas black each frame and the
   push sends all 466 rows. Little to gain while shapes cover most of the
   screen, but worth a check on the frames where they do not.

## Not measured yet

* PSRAM against an idle build, a lap soak with the rotation on, and a long run.
  PSRAM was flat at 7,327,227 in every capture and heap held at 322,648-323,056
  bytes over 45 seconds.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-7/deluxe-ideas-for-more-than-11-13-fps","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-7-deluxe-ideas-for-more-than-11-13-fps","createdAt":"2026-10-10T14:55:15.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:45.802Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Enhancement","hack","Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver"],"attachments":[{"id":"2e9ea338-3a1b-4486-a244-a095db111a6f","title":"#54 Deluxe: ideas for more than 11-13 fps","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/54"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

   the per-pixel work. Long runs go through one call per run.
4. **Draw a star as one polygon.** A star is ten segments plus ten joins
   today. Filling its outline once would mean far fewer fills and no mask.
5. **Single precision in** `draw_star`**.** It does ten `cos` and ten `sin` in
   software `double` per star per frame. Small beside the rest, but a
   single-precision wrapper is cheap (`techniques.md`).
6. **Cheaper erase.** The hack fills the whole canvas black each frame and the
   push sends all 466 rows. Little to gain while shapes cover most of the
   screen, but worth a check on the frames where they do not.

## Not measured yet

* PSRAM against an idle build, a lap soak with the rotation on, and a long run.
  PSRAM was flat at 7,327,227 in every capture and heap held at 322,648-323,056
  bytes over 45 seconds.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-7/deluxe-ideas-for-more-than-11-13-fps","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-7-deluxe-ideas-for-more-than-11-13-fps","createdAt":"2026-10-10T14:55:15.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:45.802Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Enhancement","hack","Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver"],"attachments":[{"id":"2e9ea338-3a1b-4486-a244-a095db111a6f","title":"#54 Deluxe: ideas for more than 11-13 fps","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/54"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

{"id":"ARS-8","uuid":"1528592d-6d68-49b5-a509-9b89e9b9cd9f","title":"Do Pacman and Celtic hit the stroker's gaps and overpaint that Deluxe did?","description":"Deluxe (#55) turned up two problems in the shim's wide-line stroker. This is
to find out whether Pacman and Celtic have them too. Nothing here has been
measured on either hack yet.

## What Deluxe showed

* **Gaps.** `XDrawArc` with a wide GC strokes the arc as a polyline in
  `stroke_polyline`. For a full circle (box 160, width 30, butt caps, miter
  joins) the pixel at (57, 31), radius 80.6 in a band from 65 to 95, is left
  empty. A row-by-row ring, `stroke_circle`, fills it. The first Deluxe frames
  had ragged circle edges from this. The cause is not known: it could be the
  miter joins, the point spacing or the quad edges.
* **Cost.** A 700 pixel circle of width 50 is about a thousand short wide
  segments, each filled a row at a time, so each pixel was painted about 25
  times. That was 94% of a Deluxe frame (2-5 fps), and the ring removed it
  (13-15 fps).

## What Pacman and Celtic do

Read from the source, not run:

* **Pacman** draws its maze walls with `XDrawArc` through `stippledGC`, set to
  `wallwidth` (`(xs + ys) >> 4`), `CapRound` and `JoinMiter`. The arcs are
  90 degree quarters (`pacman.c` lines 638-662), so `stroke_circle`, which
  only does full circles, does not apply. It runs at 75-79 fps, so cost is not
  its problem, but a gap in a wall corner would be a visual one.
* **Celtic** strokes its curves as wide lines with `CapRound` and `JoinRound`
  (`curve_width`, `shadow_width`). Its one `XDrawArc` is a 10 pixel node
  marker with a thin GC, so arcs are not why it is slow. Its wide round-capped
  curves are many short wide segments, which is the pattern that cost Deluxe
  its frame rate. #37 has its device numbers (1.2 fps).

## To do

1. Dump Pacman frames at several counts and look at the wall corners for
   broken or ragged joins. Dump Celtic's curves the same way.
2. Find what leaves the gap. A test that draws a wide full arc and checks that
   every pixel inside the band is set would fail today (it is the reverse of
   `test_stroke_circle_fills_the_band_between_its_two_radii`).
3. Profile Celtic as Deluxe was profiled: host time with the wide-line calls
   switched off, then split the step on the device (host time misled us on
   Braid). Check how much is overpaint from overlapping segment and join
   quads before looking at anything else.
4. If the stroker is the cause, fix it in `stroke.c`, not in a hack. Any change
   to shared stroke code can move the pinned frames of Braid, Pacman and
   Celtic, so re-pin them only after looking at the frames, and ask Rod first.

{"id":"ARS-9","uuid":"d6344ec5-0ad4-45db-9b25-95881da7ced2","title":"Pacman: measure the internal heap cost of per-pixmap dirty arrays","description":"Filed by Claude, working for Rod.

## Question

Since #64, every colour pixmap is a `Canvas`. Besides its pixels, each one
carries two dirty-span arrays (`int16_t` per row, so 4 bytes per row), which
nothing ever reads for a pixmap. How much internal heap does that cost
Pacman, which holds many small sprite pixmaps?

## Why it might matter

* The arrays come from plain `malloc`. Small blocks stay in internal SRAM on
  the ESP32-S3, so unlike the pixels of a large pixmap they don't go to PSRAM.
  Internal heap is the scarce one: about 318 KB free while Truchet runs, and
  Celtic was shelved partly for holding 300 KB of it (#37).
* Pacman scales its sprite sheet into pixmaps at start, so it holds the most
  pixmaps of any registered hack.

## What is known

* In the `ROTATE_SECONDS=5` capture for #64, Pacman's heap reading was the
  same on every visit after the first lap, so nothing leaks.
* It wasn't compared with `main` before #64, so the size of the cost is
  unknown.

## To measure

1. Flash `main` from before #64 (`5b8f8fb`) and `main` after it, each pinned
   to Pacman with rotation off, and read `heap=` from the serial log. A boot
   is deterministic, so compare the two builds window by window.
2. If the difference is large, either skip the dirty arrays for pixmap
   canvases (let `mark_span` do nothing when they are NULL) or allocate them
   from PSRAM.

Related: #61, #64.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-9/pacman-measure-the-internal-heap-cost-of-per-pixmap-dirty-arrays","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-9-pacman-measure-the-internal-heap-cost-of-per-pixmap-dirty","createdAt":"2026-10-10T23:37:32.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:48.709Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["hack","Performance","Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver"],"attachments":[{"id":"9e5ae67c-89c3-464f-ac59-4c778f00604d","title":"#65 Pacman: measure the internal heap cost of per-pixmap dirty arrays","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/65"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

{"id":"ARS-11","uuid":"63447ce2-9c38-484e-9df9-7d54f3310080","title":"Hexadrop: about 10 fps, bound by PSRAM canvas writes","description":"Filed by Claude (an agent working under Rod's direction) during the
Flurry/Halo/Hexadrop/StonerView/XMatrix batch.

## What

Hexadrop is ported and correct but runs at about 10 fps on the device, under
the 15 fps bar.

## What was measured

| Build | fps | step |
| -- | -- | -- |
| As copied (double) | 2.2-2.6 | 377-442 ms |
| Single precision | 3.0-3.2 | 282-313 ms |
| Float convex fill (hack-local) | 9.0-9.2 | 76-79 ms |
| Two-pixel stores (registered) | 10.2 | 64-66 ms |

Splitting the step with a temporary probe: with the pixel writes skipped the
step is 0.1 ms, and with the whole fill skipped it is also 0.1 ms. So the
maths, the edge walk and the sin/cos are negligible, and the rest is canvas
writes: about 430k pixels (860 KB) a frame into the PSRAM canvas, with the push
(32.5 ms) on top. 32-bit stores only moved it 16 percent, so it is not the
store count; the likely cost is PSRAM cache-line fills from many small
scattered row writes (about 480 polygons of about 25 rows each).

## Ideas, not tried

* Record each frame's polygons and rasterise them in bands of about 8 rows, so
  writes sweep memory instead of jumping a row stride per scanline.
* A faster shared `canvas_fill_polygon`: it divides in double per edge per row
  (software maths on the S3). Hexadrop's wrapper has its own float fill, but
  other polygon hacks do not. Shared code, so it needs Rod's say-so, and any
  rounding change would move pinned frames.

The same lesson cost Halo a first attempt (its window-sized circles were
millions of PSRAM writes as colour pixmaps; packed bit planes fixed it).

Code: `firmware/src/hacks/hexadrop_single.c`.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/arsecandle/issue/ARS-11/hexadrop-about-10-fps-bound-by-psram-canvas-writes","gitBranchName":"rod-linear/ars-11-hexadrop-about-10-fps-bound-by-psram-canvas-writes","createdAt":"2026-10-11T03:11:28.000Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-19T23:27:50.342Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["hack","Performance","Migrated","stopwatch-screensaver"],"attachments":[{"id":"b8a7f27b-1dec-408e-81c9-07e1e3676125","title":"#71 Hexadrop: about 10 fps, bound by PSRAM canvas writes","subtitle":null,"url":"https://github.com/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/71"}],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Rod Begbie","createdById":"353935bc-7f62-49c9-a552-025dd561118c","team":"Arsecandle Industries","teamId":"786dc04b-a9f5-4ee1-954f-1e411a9f3981"}

{"id":"ARS-12","uuid":"69275064-7872-4273-98ef-54749b7d1773","title":"Hypnowheel: 1.4 fps, bound by additively blended pixel fill","description":"Filed by Claude (an agent working under Rod's direction) during the
Goop/Loop/Starfish/Qix/Hypnowheel/FireworkX batch.

## What

Hypnowheel is ported and renders correctly but runs at 1.4 fps on the device
(step 720 ms), far under the 15 fps bar. Nothing in the hack's own settings
fixes it.

## What was measured

| Build | fps | step |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Registered (4 layers, 13 arms) | 1.4 | 720 ms |
| `*layers: 1` | 4.4 | 200 ms |
| `*count: 5` (about 7x fewer triangles, same area) | 2.0 | 511 ms |

The probes were temporary registry overrides, since reverted. From them, about
70 percent of the step is additively blended pixel fill (435k pixels at about
1.2 us each) and about 30 percent is per-triangle setup (about 35 us each, 5,900
triangles). `tools/gl_budget.py` predicted 359 ms; it understates blended fill
by about 2x here.

## Ideas, not tried

* A faster `GL_ONE, GL_ONE` span in the patched TinyGL (the canvas pixels are
  RGB565, so a saturating add can be done two pixels at a time with masks).
* Render the GL framebuffer at half the width and height and upscale in
  `glshim`, as `hacks/lowrez_put.h` does for Fireworkx (a quarter of the
  pixels). Both change shared GL code, so they need Rod's say-so.

70 percent of the step is additively blended pixel fill (435k pixels at about
1.2 us each) and about 30 percent is per-triangle setup (about 35 us each, 5,900
triangles). `tools/gl_budget.py` predicted 359 ms; it understates blended fill
by about 2x here.

## Ideas, not tried

* A faster `GL_ONE, GL_ONE` span in the patched TinyGL (the canvas pixels are
  RGB565, so a saturating add can be done two pixels at a time with masks).
* Render the GL framebuffer at half the width and height and upscale in
  `glshim`, as `hacks/lowrez_put.h` does for Fireworkx (a quarter of the
  pixels). Both change shared GL code, so they need Rod's say-so.

{"id":"ARS-13","uuid":"9cd5a551-2627-4b49-abc3-907b36cf8e9d","title":"ad-flyingtoasters: investigate playing the original flap soundtrack","description":"Filed by Claude (an agent working under Rod's direction) after
ad-flyingtoasters landed (#83).

## What

Investigate playing the original Flying Toasters soundtrack on the board's
speaker. The board has an ES8311 audio codec and an amplifier (see the
`m5stack-stopwatch` skill); nothing in the firmware plays sound yet.

## What the original does

Read from the After Dark 2.0 module's 68000 code during the port:

* It plays only when After Dark's sound extension is present.
* Three sampled sounds in the module's resource fork play back to back:
  `snd ` 128 "Flap 1", 129 "Flap 2" and 130 "Mix 1".
* The first is Flap 1. Each next one is chosen at random, never the same as
  the one before.
* The next sound starts when the current one's length has passed. It is a
  soundtrack, not tied to individual toasters.

## Constraints

* Like the sprites, the sounds are Berkeley Systems' and must never be
  committed. `tools/after_dark_sprites.py` and the pre-script would extract
  them at build time from the user's own disk image, alongside the art.
* The `snd ` resources are probably format 1 sampled sounds (8-bit unsigned
  PCM at a Mac rate such as 22,254 Hz). Check their headers before deciding
  on a conversion.
* Playback must not cost frame time: ad-flyingtoasters at 2× is already
  blit-bound at about 21 fps (#82).

## Questions to answer

* How to drive the ES8311 and the amplifier from this Arduino/M5Unified
  build (M5Unified's `Speaker` may already cover it), and what it costs in
  RAM and CPU.
* Whether sound should be on by default for a badge worn in a room, and how
  to turn it off (a build flag, the button, or a volume setting).

input.title: Port Circuit (GL), using the GL_POLYGON fan from ARS-18
input.description:
Filed by Claude (an agent working under Rod's direction).

## What

Port xscreensaver's Circuit (`hacks/glx/circuit.c`, flying electronic components) as a GL hack. It is the first port to rely on the `GL_POLYGON` fan that ARS-18 puts in TinyGL, so it needs no `glBegin` wrapper.

## Why Circuit, not Sproingies

* One 2,100-line file, already `float` with trig tables, so little `double` cost to expect.
* Seven `GL_POLYGON` uses: two rectangles and a six-vertex seven-segment shape, all convex.
* Sproingies is eight files (six near-duplicates) and needs `glClipPlane`, which TinyGL lacks.

## Known gaps

* `glLighti` is not in TinyGL (eight calls). It is a shim gap: fill it test-first.
* `glIsEnabled` and `gluLookAt` may be missing too; the build will say.
* `gl_budget.py` could not predict it until `glLighti` exists.

## Depends on

ARS-18 (branch `feature/ARS-18-gl-polygon-fan`), which this branch stacks on.

content.content:
# X11 shim and framework gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so a hack that
  allocates arrays of it (Substrate's two 466 by 466 buffers) is twice the size
  on the host, and host leak numbers are twice the device's. On the device,
  plain `malloc`/`realloc` of about 868 KB reached PSRAM (free PSRAM fell by
  1.74 MB) and came back on restart; internal heap barely moved.
- The board's `malloc` is `CONFIG_SPIRAM_USE_MALLOC=y` with
  `SPIRAM_MALLOC_ALWAYSINTERNAL=4096`: a block up to 4 KB comes from internal
  RAM and falls back to PSRAM when that is full, and a bigger one goes to PSRAM
  first. An allocation fails only when PSRAM is gone, so a hack's `abort()` on
  a failed allocation is not the risk it looks. The cost of a big pattern is
  internal heap drained to near zero (Celtic read 1,792 B free) and its data
  in slower PSRAM: compare the log's `psram=` with its idle value for the
  overflow.
- `erase_window` (`erase.c`) follows upstream's contract: the first call draws
  nothing and returns a state, so a hack that waits after it (Celtic's 5 s
  `*delay2`) waits on the finished picture. The second call starts a one-second
  wipe (blinds, circle, fizzle or random lines, picked at random), each later
  call draws the next step, and the call after the second is up clears the
  window and returns NULL. Progress comes from `double_time()`, not from the
  call count, so the wipe lasts a second at any step rate. A test or tool
  that does not sleep for a hack's delay must install a clock
  (`xshim_set_clock`), or a wipe never ends. Six hacks never call
  `eraser_free`, so the display tracks live states and the runner releases
  them when a hack stops.
- xlockmore hacks (the 40 that include `xlockmore.h`) need `-DSTANDALONE`,
  which every PlatformIO env and `score_hacks.py` set; without it they
  include `xlock.h` instead. The envs also define `HAVE_MOBILE`, because
  otherwise each hack's `XSCREENSAVER_LINK` defines the same global
  `xscreensaver_function_table` and two hacks fail to link; the only other
  effect is an inert `*ignoreRotation: True` default. Register one in
  `hacks/registry.c` with `XLOCKMORE_HACK(<name>, "<Class>")`. The runner runs
  the hack's `setup_cb` once and passes `setup_arg` as `init_cb`'s hidden third
  argument, as xscreensaver's `screenhack.c` does. Its table is empty until
  then. Resources the framework reads but a hack does not define
  (`delta3d`, `size`, ...) fall back to `kFrameworkDefaults` in
  `x11shim/resources.c`. A `HackEntry`'s `overrides` list beats the hack's own
  defaults (Galaxy runs with `count: -3`, at most three galaxies; a count of
  -2 or above skips the hack's restart cleanup and leaks); register it with
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`. Galaxy, Drift, Discrete and Flame are built through
  `hacks/<name>_single.c`, which includes the framework headers, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h` (`double` and the libm calls become `float` and
  the `f` versions; the S3's FPU is single-precision only), then the unmodified
  hack; the original `.c` is excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`.
- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1), arcs and pixmap writes live in
  `x11shim/stroke.c`, `arc.c` and `pixmap.c`. Width 0 and 1 keep the old
  `canvas_line` path, so hacks that set no wide width are pixel-identical (every
  hack's frame is pinned in `test_hacks.c`). Braid is the one registered hack
  that draws wide lines (random width 1-7; Maze's width 2 is under
  `HAVE_JWXYZ`). A round-capped segment draws a disc at each end, so
  `stroke.c` keeps each width's rows in a table (widths to 16) rather than
  calling `canvas_fill_ellipse` (which used to do `double` maths per row, in
  software on the S3; see below). A test pins the pixels to
  `canvas_fill_ellipse`.
- `canvas_fill_ellipse` and `canvas_fill_polygon` work in whole numbers, not
  double (the S3 does double in software). The ellipse is exact: a pixel is in
  when `dx2^2 * h^2 <= w^2 * (h^2 - dy2^2)` with distances doubled, and a float
  `sqrt` only starts the search for each row (it is wrong by one at 220 by 21,
  264 by 23, 312 by 25 and 318 by 181, which the tests pin). The polygon steps
  each edge's crossing with a quotient and remainder, no division per row, and
  a pixel on a left edge is in and one on a right edge is out. The old double
  fill was not consistent at exact ties (a 45 degree edge through integer
  vertices): it left stray hatch marks on Qix's thin sliver polygons, so Qix
  (612 pixels) and Pedal (3) re-pinned. Sizes or coordinates past 32768 and
  2^24 keep the double code. On the board (step, before to after): Bouboule
  14.5 to 5.2 ms (27.4 to 36.8 fps), Qix 14.6 to 1.9 ms (37.3 to 70.1 fps),
  Pedal 21.8 to 8.6 ms (it then holds the picture for 5 s).
- A circle (`w == h`, up to 32) keeps its rows in a table by diameter, relative
  to its corner: the centre column is `2x + w - 1` and `floor_half(2x + k)` is
  `x + floor_half(k)`, so the rows do not depend on where it sits. Integer
  rows alone took Halftone (about 1,150 dots a frame) from 5 to 9.8 fps, push
  overlap to 11.4-12.0, and the table to 14.2-14.6 (#57). The row-clip bounds
  in `fill_cached_circle` are speed guards only, since `hspan` clips: removing
  them is an equivalent mutant, as is reversing the rows (a circle is symmetric).
- Lisa was the counter-example to "the stroker maths is the cost" (#98), and
  then the maths turned out to be the cost after all. Converting a slanted
  segment's ends from int to float moved it by nothing (52.1 ms either way),
  and with the line calls compiled out its step is 5.2 ms, so 47 ms of 52 was
  drawing: 1,396 segments and 6.7k spans a frame at width 2, 13k spans at
  width 8. The guess was a PSRAM cache miss per scattered span. The real
  cost was `fill_convex`: the S3 has no float divide, min, max, floor or
  64-bit conversion, so its per-row loop (two divides, `fminf`, `fmaxf`, two
  `floorf` and two `__fixsfdi` calls a row) was about 3 us a span. It now
  divides each edge's slope once per polygon and uses compares and 32-bit
  `floor_int`. That rounds a few ulps differently from dividing first, which
  moved pixels on a boundary (review of #128): a row whose span ends are within
  rounding of a boundary decision is worked out the old way, and the pixels
  match main's. Test it with each stroke on a cleared canvas
  (`test_wide_strokes_of_random_lines_match_the_pinned_hash`, pinned from main's
  rasteriser): a hash of strokes drawn together missed it, because later strokes
  covered the pixels that differed. Checking every edge of every row cost most
  of the gain (Lisa 43 ms at width 2); checking the two span ends and reusing
  their floors keeps it. On the board Lisa's step went 52.3 to 38.5 ms at width
  2 (14.2 to 17.7 fps) and 85.4 to 60.1 ms at width 8 (9.7 to 12.9 fps), Braid
  125.4 to about 94 ms (8.1 to 9.7 fps) and Deluxe 51.9 to 49.2 ms (19.0 to
  19.9 fps), two rounds each. The width
  sweep on the host (`-DLW=N` with `LINEWIDTH` edited, temporarily) shows the
  cliff is thin to wide: width 1 takes the `canvas_line` path at 0.09 ms, width
  2 is 0.52 ms and width 8 0.85 ms. Look for the same library calls in a
  per-row or per-pixel loop of any hack: `nm` on the object lists them
  (`__divsf3`, `__fixsfdi`, `floorf`, `sqrtf`).
- `canvas_line` (thin lines, width 0 and 1) keeps its endpoints as ints when
  nothing is clipped: it used to convert all four to double and back, which
  the S3 does in software, on every call. Pixels are
  unchanged (`test_lines_inside_the_canvas_match_the_reference` and the
  off-canvas twin draw 20,000 lines each, alone, with `canvas_line` and with a
  copy of the old one in the test file). Compare against a reference copy, not
  a pinned hash, for anything that goes through `clip_line`: its double
  arithmetic rounds differently when the compiler contracts to FMA, and a hash
  taken on one setting fails on the other. On the board XRaySwarm's step went
  21.05 to 13.20 ms (23.2 to 28.3 fps; about 9,700 short lines a step);
  Wormhole 26.9 to 26.0 ms and NerveRot 48.2 to 46.7 ms barely move, since
  they draw far fewer lines and clip some.
  Counting calls on the host (a scratch copy with counters in `canvas_line`,
  `arc_points`, `compute_closed_spline`) put 29 of 109 hacks on `canvas_line`.
  The colour-map builders in `helpers.c` run at start only, so their double
  maths does not matter per frame.
- `canvas_line`'s clip (`clip_line_integer`, `canvas.c`) is the Liang-Barsky
  clip in exact `int64` rationals: it compares the quotients by
  cross-multiplying and rounds each end with one integer divide. The double
  clip (`clip_line`) still decides two cases, and `canvas_line` falls back to
  it for them: an end exactly on a half pixel, where double rounding can land
  either side, and a coordinate past 2^20. The limit comes from an error bound
  (double's error stays near 1e-10, while a rational answer that is not
  exactly on a boundary is at least 1 / 2^22 from it), not from a test: a
  raised limit survives the random tests, since a miss at 10^9 is about one
  in ten million lines. A clipped end sits on the canvas border, so one
  coordinate is an integer and only the other can tie. Pixels match the old
  clip in every reference test, with FMA contraction on and off (a mutant that
  treats every integer as a tie falls back every time and so also passes). On
  the board XSpirograph's step went 11.4 to 7.45 ms (15.2 to 16.8 fps: its
  push, 18.3 to 16.3 ms, now sets the frame) with 404 of 722 lines a step
  clipped; Laser 21.3 to 20.8 ms (52% clipped, but about 270 pixels a line);
  Deco unchanged at 34.3 ms (its own delay holds it at 0.2 fps).
- `arc_points` (`arc.c`) and `compute_closed_spline` (`spline.c`) take a fast
  path and keep the old arithmetic for what the fast path cannot settle. Both
  match the old code point for point in the reference tests, with FMA
  contraction on and off; the pinned frame of every hack is unchanged.
  - `compute_closed_spline` works each point's blend of four controls in
    float (the weights are worked out once, in double, then kept as float) and
    keeps it unless it is within about 1e-3 plus 2e-6 of the largest control
    from a half pixel, where `lround` could go either way; then the original
    double expression decides. Controls past 1e6 in size take the double path
    throughout. The controls are `double` because hacks fill them in, so the
    conversion to float is once a call, not once a point. Goop: step 45.3 to
    35.4 ms (15.9 to 18.9 fps), about 500 points a step.
  - `arc_points` works a run of 16 points from the first by rotating through
    the step between points (four multiplies and two adds, not a divide, `sinf`
    and `cosf`), and a point within 2e-3 plus 4e-5 of the radius from a rounding
    boundary is worked out as before, and the rotation reseeded from it. Angles
    past 32 radians (float's spacing is then near a millionth of a radian) and
    coordinates or radii past 1e6 take the plain loop. The run length is a
    margin: the real drift over a thousand points is about 1e-3 px against a
    tolerance of 0.02 px, so a longer run passes the tests too. Piecewise:
    step 43.4 to 38.6 ms (22.4 to 25.0 fps, about 3,200 arc points a step);
    BoxFit 14.1 to 12.9 ms, with its fps flat (19.1 to 19.2) because its own
    delay sets the frame.
  - A mutant that drops the near-half fallback, one that flips a rotation
    sign, and ones that remove the angle or coordinate limits are each killed
    by the reference tests; a pinned hash would not do here either, since the
    float and double paths can round a half pixel differently.
- `single_precision.h` renames the keyword `double`, not literals: `0.5 * x`
  is still software double. Braid's wrapper includes a copy of the hack with
  every decimal literal suffixed `f`, written at build time by
  `firmware/patch_float_literals.py` (`tools/float_literals.py`). Check a
  wrapper's object for `__muldf3` and friends with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm`.
  `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` does that for every object in
  the device build, by function: a count in a per-frame function is a literal
  or a macro the header could not reach. It lists none in Galaxy, Discrete,
  Drift, Flame, Substrate or Interaggregate now.
- Four things hide soft double from `single_precision.h`, each found by that
  report. `frand` (`single_frand.h`) and `MAXRAND`, `M_PI`, `M_PI_2` and
  `M_PI_4` (`single_constants.h`) are macros with a decimal literal in their
  body, past the literal pass; both headers are opt-in, since each moves the
  wrapper's frames and pins. Exponent literals (`1e-6`, `1.0E5`) were skipped
  by `float_literals.py` until Drift and Flame showed one each. A struct
  declared with `double` fields before the rename keeps them, so a float
  `corners[j].x * size` plus a `double` `pos.x` is a software add: HexTrail's
  `XYZ` (from `normals.h`) was 94 calls in `draw_hextrail`. Give the hack its
  own float struct under the same name, and `normals.h` another name for the
  double one (`hextrail_single_gl.c`; frames byte-identical). And a trig
  argument that is a big whole number cannot be a float: XSpirograph's second
  angle is millions of degrees and Vines' is an `int` in the billions, so a
  plain `double` to `float` turned both pictures to noise. XSpirograph reduces
  its angles mod 360 in integers at build time (`tools/xspirograph_patch.py`);
  Vines builds `(double) a` as `(long) a`, so its `cos` macro gets the exact
  integer and takes the phase as a 64-bit multiply by 2^64 / 2 pi, wrapping
  into whole turns (`vines_single.c`). Look at a frame before trusting a
  float build of anything whose angles grow. To find the line of a stray
  promotion, add `-Wdouble-promotion -fsyntax-only` to a file's compile
  command in `firmware/compile_commands.json` (`pio run -e stopwatch -t
  compiledb`; delete the file afterwards, it upsets the editor).
- A colour pixmap is a `Canvas`, and every drawing primitive draws on the
  drawable it is given (`xshim_target` in `pixmap.c`); `None` draws nothing,
  and a bitmap takes only `XCopyArea`, `XCopyPlane` and filled rectangles and
  polygons (see below). One exception still draws on the window whatever
  it is given: Deluxe's wrapper, which calls `stroke_circle(dpy->canvas,
  ...)`. No
  registered hack drew into a pixmap before this (the `HAVE_JWXYZ` wrappers
  and Deluxe's `doubleBuffer: False` turn double-buffering off), so keep
  those: a back buffer costs 434 KB and a full-frame copy, and dirties every
  row. Without a
  clip mask, `XCopyArea` copies colour rows whole with `canvas_paste_rect`. A
  pixmap wider or taller than `INT16_MAX` is `None` (the canvas's dirty spans
  are `int16_t`). Truchet draws into one (issue #61). The display tracks every
  pixmap a hack holds and the runner frees what a stopped hack left behind
  (Pacman leaked 514 KB per start). The GC keeps its own copy of a clip mask
  because hacks free the pixmap right after `XSetClipMask`. There is no PNG
  decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads
  the raw blob described in `ximage-loader.h`, made by
  `tools/make_logo_blob.py` (`uv run`, needs Pillow). Pacman's sprites,
  XMatrix's large glyph sheets and the grab image are built with `--deflate`

  buffer while the image loads (Pacman's is 522 KB of PSRAM, briefly), by the
  ROM's `tinfl` on the device and zlib on the host, so host builds link `-lz`

  an earlier probe would survive. The logo shows in Maze only.

  segments, each filled a row at a time: 40 times the fills of a ring, and the

- `XshimGC.alpha` (0 is opaque, 1 to 31 is the weight out of 32) makes the

- Don't declare `xrealloc` or `xmalloc` in the shim: cloudlife defines its own
